tier_reason: Benchmark code is public (tools/resize/tests/tir_bench.c, Makefile target resize-bench) and the CPU is named (Ryzen 9 3950X), but the README never states the compiler (the recipe uses $(CC); GNU make's built-in CC=cc is not overridden by 'CC ?= gcc', version unknown), the stb_image_resize2 header is fetched on demand and not version-pinned, and the recipe compiles stb2 at baseline SSE2 (-O2 -g, no -mavx/-mavx2/-mfma) while tir dispatches AVX2+FMA at runtime, so the comparison with the named baseline is not like-for-like; first-party numbers with that methodology gap are C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README Performance tables (output MP/s of f32 pixels, one AVX2 core, Ryzen 9 3950X, Mitchell 4-tap), tir AVX2 / exr_v3 / stb2. 4-channel: 2x up 295 / 135 / 266; 2x down 78 / 30 / 73; 7.3x down 7.6 / 2.2 / 6.4. 1-channel: 2x up 1218 / 443 / 1279; 2x down 334 / 92 / 365; 7.3x down 27.3 / 8.2 / 25.4. Ratios vs stb2 (derived from page data): 4-channel 1.11x, 1.07x, 1.19x; 1-channel 0.95x (2x up), 0.92x (2x down, stb2 about 9% faster, more than the README's 'within ~5%'), 1.07x (7.3x down). Ratios vs tinyexr's own exr_resize_float (derived from page data): 2.2x to 3.6x. Author text: 'tir beats exr_resize_float 2-5x everywhere' and 'Against stb2 (matched filters) tir wins on every 4-channel case'; the triangle-filter rows the author also cites are not in the README table.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Makefile target resize-bench: $(CC) -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -O2 -g (CFLAGS is not used by this recipe), no -march/-mavx/-mavx2/-mfma; the Makefile line 'CC ?= gcc' does not override GNU make's built-in default CC=cc, so the compiler is the system cc, name and version not stated in the README. tir's AVX2/FMA kernels are compiled with __attribute__((target(...))) in tools/resize/src/tir_kernels_x86.c and selected at runtime by CPUID (tir_cpu.c); stb_image_resize2.h picks SIMD at compile time (AVX/AVX2 only when __AVX__/__AVX2__ or STBIR_AVX/STBIR_AVX2 are defined), so under this recipe stb2 runs its SSE2 path. stb2 is enabled with make resize-bench STB=1 (-DTIR_BENCH_STB) after dropping the header into tools/resize/tests/.
corrections.caveats: The win over the named baseline is small and not like-for-like: the bench recipe builds stb_image_resize2 without -mavx/-mavx2/-mfma, so stb2 ran its SSE2 kernels while tir used runtime-dispatched AVX2+FMA; stb_image_resize2's own header says AVX is 10-40% faster and AVX2 about another 12%, which exceeds tir's 7-19% 4-channel lead, so tir may not beat an AVX2 build of stb2. On 1-channel Mitchell stb2 is faster in the two 2x cases (0.95x and 0.92x, derived from page data). The workload does matched work: Mitchell B=C=1/3 on both sides, clamp edges on both sides (tir default TIR_EDGE_CLAMP, stb STBIR_EDGE_CLAMP), straight alpha on tir and STBIR_4CHANNEL (no alpha weighting) on stb, f32 in and out, random data, one-shot calls that build coefficients each time; the bench does not compare outputs, and tir's SIMD kernels may reassociate sums within a small ULP budget. The Lanczos3 row compares against a 4-tap Catmull-Rom on the stb side and is excluded. The 2-5x figure is against tinyexr's own exr_resize_float, not an outside incumbent. Author-run on a single Zen 2 machine; the stb2 header version used is not recorded (gitignored, fetched on demand). tir is new (first commit 2026-07-02, last change to tools/resize 2026-07-05), developed with an AI co-author, version 0.x.

notes: README numbers and the derived ratios match the page; the 'fair stb2 bench' commit d480dc7 fixed an earlier filter mismatch, but the ISA mismatch remains because the resize-bench recipe ignores CFLAGS and passes no -m flags. A rerun of stb2 with -mavx2 -mfma (or -DSTBIR_AVX2) would be needed before this can carry A or claim a win over stb_image_resize2.

tier_reason: First-party only: README states '2x - 3x' on an i7-10750H and the chart's raw timings are hard-coded in py/performance.ipynb, but the C++ driver that timed cv::blur is not in the repo and the OpenCV version, build (IPP, threads) and benchmark flags are not stated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README Performance: 'designed to be a portable, easy, and faster replacement of cv::blur, using an i7-10750H, it's around 2x - 3x time faster'. The chart data (py/performance.ipynb, times in ms for 45 RGB 8-bit images from 1500x1000 to 11400x7600, box size 2*width-1): 1 pass cv::blur 20.2 to 1900.6 ms vs fastboxblur 15.9 to 650.8 ms; 2 passes cv::blur 39.3 to 3970.2 ms vs fastboxblur 23.6 to 1180.7 ms. Speedups (derived from page data): 1 pass 1.27x to 2.92x (median 2.62x), 2 passes 1.49x to 3.36x (median 2.90x), rising with image size.
corrections.workload: Box blur with reflect-101 style mirror padding (edge sample not repeated, like OpenCV's default BORDER_REFLECT_101) on 45 synthetic-size RGB 8-bit images from 1500x1000 to 11400x7600, box size 2*width-1, 1 and 2 passes; FastBoxBlur does horizontal sliding-sum passes, a blocked transpose, vertical passes as horizontal passes, and a transpose back (timings listed in py/performance.ipynb, plot in data/bench.png).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Repo Makefile (the only build in the repo; the benchmark build is not stated): g++ fastboxblur.cpp -O3 -fopenmp -std=c++17. The OpenCV side's version, compiler and build options are not stated.
corrections.caveats: Likely threads-versus-one-thread: fast_box_blur.h parallelises every horizontal pass and the transpose with '#pragma omp parallel for' and the Makefile builds with -fopenmp, so on the 6-core/12-thread i7-10750H FastBoxBlur probably ran on all hardware threads, while OpenCV 4.x's CPU cv::blur goes through boxFilter's single-threaded FilterEngine (no parallel_for_ in box_filter.dispatch.cpp or filter.dispatch.cpp) unless a HAL intercepts it; the 1.3-3.4x lead is smaller than the thread count, so per-core FastBoxBlur may not be faster. The cv::blur driver is not in the repo, so the OpenCV version, IPP/HAL build, setNumThreads value and exact cv::blur arguments cannot be checked. The kernel size 2*width-1 is extreme (thousands of pixels); OpenCV's FilterEngine pads each row by the kernel radius, so this size inflates OpenCV's border work, and typical small kernels were not measured. FastBoxBlur clamps the radius to dimension-1 per axis (r = min(r, w-1)), so on landscape images its vertical kernel is smaller than a cv::blur call given the same square ksize would use; whether the benchmark matched that is unknown. Integer accumulation with float normalisation and +0.5 rounding; output equivalence with cv::blur is not tested in the repo. Borderline for color-and-resampling (a convolution filter, not a resampler). MIT is stated only in the README; there is no LICENSE file. Last commit 2022-11-01; 5 stars.

notes: The per-size chart data is readable as text in py/performance.ipynb (hard-coded timings), which supports the README's 2x-3x on large images but shows only 1.27x at 1500x1000. The OpenMP-versus-single-threaded-OpenCV concern is strong enough that the orchestrator may want to note it as the main shortcoming.

tier_reason: First-party claim only: the README gives a bare '25-100%' range against OpenCV with no per-case numbers, CPU, OpenCV version or thread settings, and main.cpp times KLERP alone (2x2 to 800x2000, multithreaded) without running OpenCV.

corrections.caveats: Only the percentage range appears in the README (and the identical header comment in KLERP.h and main.cpp). main.cpp is a KLERP-only timing loop (2000 warm-ups and 2000 runs, 2x2 image upscaled to 800x2000, multithreading=true) and never calls OpenCV, so the comparison cannot be reproduced from the repo. CPU, OpenCV version and OpenCV build options (IPP, thread count) are not stated. KLERP spawns std::thread::hardware_concurrency() threads for outputs of 20000 pixels or more; OpenCV's resize is also parallelised with parallel_for_ by default, so threading is probably comparable, but this is not documented. Grayscale 8-bit only and AVX2 required; output is designed to match OpenCV's fixed-point bilinear ('silliness to match opencv's output' in KLERP.h). Code dates from 2016-12-26 (the only later commit, 2021-03-23, added the LICENSE), so the OpenCV compared against was probably 3.x; OpenCV has since reworked resize with wide universal intrinsics, so the lead may have shrunk or vanished.

notes: Record is accurate; metadata checked (MIT LICENSE file, 23 stars, 9 forks, two commits, last 2021-03-23, abandoned). Resize fits the category, unlike the box blur.
